J.J. Gibson

James J. Gibson (1904–1979) posed the most radical alternative to the world-modeling framework 1, 2. Perception does not require internal representations, inference, or models. The structured ambient light array (optic flow, texture gradients, occlusion patterns) already contains sufficient information to specify the layout of the environment directly. Organisms do not build models; they pick up affordances—possibilities for action offered by the environment. Gibson’s ecological approach remains a powerful critique: any computational theory of world modeling must explain what it can do that direct specification cannot.

Hilary Putnam

Hilary Putnam (1926–2016) introduced functionalism, the thesis that mental states are individuated not by their physical substrate but by their functional roles—their causal relations to sensory inputs, behavioral outputs, and other mental states 3, 4. Multiple realizability—the argument that the same mental state could in principle be implemented in neurons, silicon, or any other medium with the right functional organization—licenses computational neuroscience’s focus on algorithms over hardware. Putnam later turned against his own position, arguing in Representation and Reality 5 that computational functionalism cannot adequately capture meaning.

Jerry Fodor

Jerry Fodor (1935–2017) articulated the classical computational theory of cognition. The Language of Thought 6 argued that thinking is computation over structured symbolic representations in an innate mental language (“Mentalese”). The Modularity of Mind 7 proposed that perceptual systems are informationally encapsulated, domain-specific, fast, and mandatory modules—a claim that continues to shape theories of cortical functional architecture, even as strict encapsulation is challenged by the top-down predictions of predictive processing.

David Marr

David Marr (1945–1980) provided the methodological framework that computational neuroscience still largely operates within. In Vision [Vision], he argued that any information-processing system must be understood at three levels: the computational level (what problem is being solved and why?), the algorithmic level (what representations and processes are used?), and the implementational level (how are these physically realized?). Before asking how the brain builds a world model, one must first specify what a world model is for.

Thomas Nagel

Thomas Nagel (1937–) raised a challenge that no computational theory has fully met. “What Is It Like to Be a Bat?” 8 argues that an organism has conscious experience if there is something it is like to be that organism. Even a complete physical, functional, and computational description of a bat’s sonar system would not convey what echolocation feels like from the bat’s own point of view. This explanatory gap between objective description and subjective experience haunts every world-modeling theory: does the model fully constitute experience, or does something remain left over?

Noam Chomsky

Noam Chomsky (1928–) precipitated the cognitive revolution with the argument that language acquisition cannot be explained by learning from environmental input alone 9, 10. The poverty of the stimulus holds that the linguistic data available to a child massively underdetermines the grammar the child reliably acquires; therefore, the mind must bring rich innate structure—a universal grammar—to the learning task. This rationalist nativism ended the dominance of behaviorism and reintroduced the Kantian insight in a new key: the brain does not learn from data alone but brings powerful structural priors that constrain and enable acquisition. In the language of predictive processing, Chomsky’s universal grammar is a highly informative prior over the space of possible generative models of language—biology’s answer to the poverty of the sensory stream.

Fred Dretske

Fred Dretske (1932–2013) developed the most influential information-theoretic account of mental representation 11, 12. A neural state represents an external condition, Dretske argued, if it carries information about that condition: that is, if there is a lawful, counterfactual-supporting dependency such that the neural state would not have occurred (during the relevant learning period) had the external condition not obtained. This naturalized intentionality by grounding the “aboutness” of mental states in objective statistical relations rather than in semantic primitives taken as given. For computational neuroscience, Dretske provides a principled criterion for what makes a pattern of neural activity a representation of something in the world: the reliable, learned covariance between internal state and external cause—precisely the kind of dependency that a well-trained generative model exploits.
